Procedural learning refers to the process of acquiring the skills needed to perform a task. When mastering a new activity—such as skiing or playing the piano—you may reach a point during practice where further effort seems to produce no additional improvement. However, upon returning to the task the next day, you often find your performance has improved noticeably. This phenomenon is typically driven by the brain’s consolidation processes that occur during sleep, rather than by merely passing time.

For instance, if you spend ten minutes repeatedly typing a specific key sequence as quickly as possible, you will usually plateau after the first five minutes. Yet, when you revisit the task the following morning, you will type faster and with greater fluidity. In contrast, if you practice in the morning and test yourself later that same evening without intervening sleep, you are unlikely to see any measurable progress. 

Not every type of sleep confers the same benefit. Research indicates that the most substantial overnight gains are associated with extended periods of Stage 2 sleep, during which brief but powerful bursts of neural activity—known as sleep spindles—occur. These spindles appear to play a key role in solidifying newly learned motor patterns.

Invertebrates exhibit a wide array of sophisticated caregiving strategies, making it challenging to trace the evolutionary origins of these behaviors. Nevertheless, several hypotheses highlight key determinants that shape parental care across species. A primary determinant is the habitat in which offspring develop. For instance, in extreme environments such as deserts, parental involvement is crucial because eggs and juveniles face severe desiccation and temperature stress, conditions that often preclude independent survival. Additionally, when food resources are limited and temporally variable, competition intensifies; in such scenarios, parental provisioning becomes essential to ensure adequate nourishment for the young. Finally, parental vigilance is frequently required to protect vulnerable offspring from predators that seek to consume them.

Another significant factor is the differential survival rates of offspring depending on parental presence. The proportion of juveniles that survive to reproductive age directly affects the number of parental alleles transmitted to subsequent generations. Consequently, higher offspring survival in the presence of parents enhances the inclusive fitness of those parents, reinforcing the adaptive value of parental care behaviors.

Because the amount of charge that can be stored depends on the surface area of the plates, many capacitors are fabricated with rolled or cylindrical geometries to maximize area while keeping the component compact. In some specialized applications, different shapes or configurations are used to meet specific performance requirements.

Even when a capacitor is not intentionally built, two conductors placed close together can exhibit a capacitive effect, creating an unplanned but measurable electric field.

Edaphology (from Greek, edaphos, "ground") is one of two main divisions of soil science, the other being pedology. Edaphology is concerned with the influence of soils on living things, particularly plants. General subfields within edaphology are agricultural soil science (known by the term agrology in some regions) and environmental soil science. In Russia, edaphology is considered equivalent to pedology, but is recognized to have an applied sense consistent with agrophysics and agrochemistry outside Russia. Xenophon (431–355 BC), and Cato (234–149 BC), were early edaphologists. Xenophon noted the beneficial effect of turning a cover crop into the earth. Cato wrote De Agri Cultura ("On Farming") which recommended tillage, crop rotation and the use of legumes in the rotation to build soil nitrogen. He also devised the first soil capability classification for specific crops.

This phenomenon was first reported in 1808 by the mathematician Étienne-Louis Malus. One can observe the effect using a polarizing filter—for example, the lenses in a pair of polarizing sunglasses. By rotating the filter while looking through it at the reflected light from a distant horizontal plane, the intensity of the reflected light will vary. At specific rotation angles, the reflected light may be greatly diminished or even disappear entirely. Polarizing filters work by blocking light that is polarized perpendicular to the filter’s transmission axis. If two polarizers are stacked so that their axes are at 90° to each other, almost no light will pass through both.

Polarization also occurs when light is scattered in the atmosphere. The scattered light is responsible for the brightness and the hues of a clear sky. Because the scattering process partially polarizes the light, photographers can use a polarizing filter to darken the sky in photographs, thereby increasing contrast. The effect is most noticeable at sunset, when the sky is viewed from the horizon at a 90° angle to the setting sun. A similar phenomenon is the marked reduction in brightness that occurs when images of the sky and clouds are reflected from horizontal surfaces.
